articles.summaryTr: A woman says an agency boss sent her to photoshoots at the sex offender's Florida beach home.
articles.articleText: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor - Published A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house. At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home. "My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service. Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models. "My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza. She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house. She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women. Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her. Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused. We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction. The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company. Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates. A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie. He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers. Sara Ziff, founder of the Model Alliance, which campaigns for stronger protections for models in the US, approves. "Often, [model agencies] are the problem. They are the link between the model and these predatory men." Roza says the person behind the camera at the photoshoots MC2 sent her to was not a professional photographer, but Epstein's girlfriend at the time, Nadia Marcinko. Roza describes the set-up as "strange - there was no stylist" and the photos were never used. She has since become convinced the shoots were stage-managed by Epstein and MC2. The Model Trap BBC Eye reveals new evidence showing how scouts, agencies and powerful fashion figures helped Jeffrey Epstein gain access to young women after his conviction for sex offences. If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, external An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier. "Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says. A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency. We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply. Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims. "Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked." In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school. The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse. Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein. We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse. Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed." He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual." - If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves. "These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do." Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times. "People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona. She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates. At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company. Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein. After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling. And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years. The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place. Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him." They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery. We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply. Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable". Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward. "There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out." Additional reporting by Annika Grosser

articles.title: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
articles.summary: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are all sending delegation to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.

articles.titleTr: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
articles.summaryTr: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are all sending delegation to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.
articles.articleText: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say - Published Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said. The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February. Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches. Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine. "An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X. But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart. A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia. Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security. While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately". However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture". "They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other." For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans. The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022. The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since. Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks. The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans." Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success. Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union. After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe". Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv. The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said. "While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war". Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky. Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya. Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms. On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations." "This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism." articles.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.summaryTr: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
articles.articleText: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise. In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON. For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared. Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011. And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK. As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between. America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels. Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet. The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills? Two decisions On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil. Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security. Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas. Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations. Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable. At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama. But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt." "We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy." There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it. The case for drilling Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!" Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field. Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks. The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills". "If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice. Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress. But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets." Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had." Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead. Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption. And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another. With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination. The case for electrons The alternative is to build. Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel. The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables. The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs. Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power. And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars. And China's lead is growing. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on. If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin. articles.summaryTr: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
articles.articleText: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy - Published Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy. The US President said he spoke with chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". Nvidia, who has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off the value of Nvidia during trading on Monday as the firm's share price fell by about 4%. Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted the BBC. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia, the company at the centre at the development of AI worldwide through its microchips. The American firm run, co-founded by Huang, is also a major focus in the AI rivalry between the US and China, with Washington officials treating the company's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security. 'He said he had no idea she was a spy' At the White House, Trump was asked multiple times, including by the BBC, on when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific. Trump said he thought Huang was an "honorable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations. "I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president said. He said he spoke with Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy". Trump added he was "sure" China president Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met. Huang has admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week. In the letter, the chairmen of the committees said they were seeking a briefing "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang". It is unclear whether Huang will appear. The BBC has contacted Nvidia and the committees. - What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published29 minutes ago - Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published2 hours ago Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent. It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today. Its chips have become so valuable to the AI-build out that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

articles.summaryTr: The billionaire tech executive finds himself mired in a personal and national security scandal.
articles.articleText: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted, external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair. The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. - Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy - Published22 minutes ago - Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published2 hours ago Who is Alice Huang and what do we know about the affair? US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported, external. Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC. China has rejected the spying allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Why does it matter? Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race, which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China. Who is Jensen Huang? Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech", he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country". What is Nvidia and how important is it? Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games. Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates. Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch. "Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC. Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips. Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever. For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team". Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy. His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles. Who is Jensen Huang's wife? Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer. In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn. Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University. Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him". "He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney - Published21 September

US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair. The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. - Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy - Published22 minutes ago - Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published2 hours ago Who is Alice Huang and what do we know about the affair? US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported, external. Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC. China has rejected the spying allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Why does it matter? Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race, which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China. Who is Jensen Huang? Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech", he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country". What is Nvidia and how important is it? Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games. Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates. Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch. "Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC. Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips. Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever. For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team". Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy. His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles. Who is Jensen Huang's wife? Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer. In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn. Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University. Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him". "He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." articles.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
articles.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process next year.

articles.titleTr: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
articles.summaryTr: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process next year.
articles.articleText: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth - Published A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution. "By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said. The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process. Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record. "You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down." He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda. Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside. "I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles. Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power. "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials." Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January. Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that". He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject. Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed. As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict. The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one. While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago. He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years. Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority. Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins. "There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said. Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House. While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term. When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 60 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office. Related topics - Published22 hours ago

articles.title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
articles.summary: The ruling means the case can move forward, possibly with reduced charges in a new trial.

articles.titleTr: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
articles.summaryTr: The ruling means the case can move forward, possibly with reduced charges in a new trial.
articles.articleText: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case - Published A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children. The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict. Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional. The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether. Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice. Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative. The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight. In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC. The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said. "Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy." Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath. He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive". The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March. The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment. Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home. After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict. The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity. In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant. Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty. Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts. Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

articles.articleText: Dana White declines Trump’s offer to be White House press secretary Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White declined President Donald Trump's offer to be the next White House press secretary during a briefing on Monday. The president had asked White to take over the role in a social post over the weekend. Trump later said he was "having a little fun". During the briefing, White confirmed he won't take the job as he doesn't "want to be in politics."

articles.summaryTr: ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, İran'a yönelik askeri müdahalenin şu an için gerekli görünmediğini söyledi. Trump, koşulların değişmesi halinde ABD ordusunun harekete geçmeye hazır olduğunu belirtti.
articles.articleText: Trump'tan İran açıklaması: "Şu aşamada askeri müdahale gerekli görünmüyor" YAYIN TARİHİ, 10 Kasım 2026 01:26 PAYLAŞ - ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, İran'a yönelik askeri müdahalenin şu an için gerekli görünmediğini söyledi. Trump, koşulların değişmesi halinde ABD ordusunun harekete geçmeye hazır olduğunu belirtti. ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, İran'la yaşanan çatışmaya ilişkin yaptığı açıklamada, şu aşamada ABD'nin askeri müdahalede bulunmasına gerek olmadığını düşündüğünü söyledi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle 9 Kasım Pazartesi günü gazetecilerin sorularını yanıtlayan Trump, "Bu noktada askeri harekât çok gerekli bir şey gibi görünmüyor. Ancak herhangi bir nedenle koşullar değişirse harekete geçmeye hazırız" ifadelerini kullandı. "Çatışmanın yakında sona ereceğini düşünüyorum" Trump, Tahran yönetimiyle yaşanan çatışmanın seyrine ilişkin de değerlendirmede bulundu. ABD Başkanı, "Bunun oldukça yakında sona ereceğini düşünüyorum" dedi. Trump'ın açıklamaları, Washington yönetiminin İran'a yönelik askeri seçenekleri tamamen dışlamadığını, ancak mevcut koşullarda doğrudan müdahaleyi gerekli görmediğini ortaya koydu.

articles.summaryTr: ABD Dışişleri Bakanı Marco Rubio, İsrail'in finansal açıdan yeterli seviyeye ulaştığını belirterek Washington yönetiminin Tel Aviv'e artık finansman sağlamasına gerek kalmadığını söyledi. İki ülke arasında yeni bir savunma mutabakatı üzerinde görüşmeler sürüyor.
articles.articleText: ABD'den İsrail'e para musluğu kapanıyor! Rubio'dan dikkat çeken açıklama - ABD Dışişleri Bakanı Marco Rubio, İsrail'in finansal açıdan yeterli seviyeye ulaştığını belirterek Washington yönetiminin Tel Aviv'e artık finansman sağlamasına gerek kalmadığını söyledi. İki ülke arasında yeni bir savunma mutabakatı üzerinde görüşmeler sürüyor. ABD Dışişleri Bakanı Marco Rubio, Fransa'nın başkenti Paris'te düzenlenen G7 Dışişleri Bakanları toplantısının ardından yaptığı açıklamada, ABD'nin İsrail'e yönelik askeri finansman politikasında değişikliğe gidilebileceğinin sinyalini verdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Rubio, ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın beklentisinin İsrail'in artık kendi finansmanını karşılayabilecek ekonomik güce ulaştığı yönünde olduğunu belirtti. Rubio, "Başkanın beklentisi, İsrail'in artık yeterince refah düzeyine ve zenginliğe ulaştığı, dolayısıyla sadece 'satış' modeline geçebileceği yönünde. Bizden silah alabilir ama artık finansman sağlamamız gerekmiyor. Zaten bu, bizzat İsrail tarafının bize önerdiği bir husus" dedi. ABD ile İsrail arasında yeni savunma anlaşması görüşmeleri ABD ve İsrail'in yeni bir mutabakat zaptı üzerinde müzakereler yürüttüğünü aktaran Rubio, İsrail'in de kendi silahlarını ürettiğine dikkat çekti. Rubio, iki ülkenin bazı savunma kalemlerinde ortak üretim modeline geçebileceğini ifade etti. Rubio'dan Hegseth'e destek Rubio, ABD Savunma Bakanı Pete Hegseth'in görevden alınabileceğine ilişkin iddialar hakkında da konuştu. Hegseth'in İran'la savaşı destekleyen isimlerden biri olduğu yönündeki değerlendirmeler ve Trump'ın kendisini görevden almayı düşündüğü iddiaları hatırlatılan Rubio, savunma bakanına destek verdi. Rubio, Hegseth'in görevinde "çok iyi iş çıkardığını" düşündüğünü söyledi. Yapay zekanın ekonomik etkilerine dikkat çekti Rubio, yapay zekanın sağladığı fırsatların yanı sıra güvenlik ve ekonomi alanlarında ciddi riskler barındırdığını belirtti. Yapay zekanın biyolojik ve kimyasal silah üretiminde, siber saldırılarda ve terör eylemlerinde kullanılabileceğine ilişkin endişelerini dile getiren Rubio, teknolojinin iş gücü üzerindeki etkilerine de dikkat çekti. Rubio, yapay zekanın ekonomik faydalar sağlayacağını ancak bazı sektörleri ve çalışanları devre dışı bırakma potansiyeli bulunduğunu söyledi. Küresel kurumların yapay zekanın gelişimini yavaşlatacak düzenlemeler arayışında olduğunu savunan Rubio, bu yaklaşımdan endişe duyduğunu ve doğru bulmadığını ifade etti.

articles.title: Here’s what happened in crypto today
articles.summary: Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.

articles.titleTr: Here’s what happened in crypto today
articles.summaryTr: Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
articles.articleText: Here’s what happened in crypto today Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation. Today in crypto, Elliptic said North Korean hackers used memecoins to launder funds stolen in the Binance hack, EU authorities asked the finance industry to develop common standards for tokenized securities, and Zcash developers proposed cutting block times from 25 to 20 seconds. North Korean hackers create memecoins to launder funds from Binance hack: Elliptic North Korean hackers created memecoins to launder cryptocurrency stolen in the $6.3 billion Binance hack, routing roughly $430,000 through six newly launched tokens on the NEAR blockchain, according to a report from blockchain analytics firm Elliptic. Between Nov. 5 and 7, the hackers created at least six tokens on NEAR and used liquidity pools on decentralized exchanges to move stolen funds between wallets, Elliptic said. The tokens attracted almost no outside trading and were abandoned shortly after launch. The hackers used one set of wallets to swap stolen NEAR tokens for the new memecoins, then used another set to sell those memecoins back into the pools for NEAR. The swaps let them move funds without direct wallet-to-wallet transfers, though the transactions remained traceable onchain. Elliptic said the same laundering technique was also used following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025, when North Korean-linked actors moved at least $24 million through a newly created token on the TRON blockchain. EU taps industry to set standards for tokenized securities The European Central Bank, European Commission and European Securities and Markets Authority are seeking nominations for an industry-led group that will draft common standards for holding and settling tokenized securities. Eligible applicants include EU industry associations, global institutions, private firms and fintech companies. They can apply to the European Tokenisation Standards Group (ETSG) by Nov. 27, with work set to begin in January 2027, according to a release published Monday. The three EU institutions will participate as observers. The group will develop technical and market standards to help companies hold and settle tokenized securities across different distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms and ensure those platforms can work with existing financial systems. The group aims to produce an initial set of standards by early 2028, according to its mandate. The standards will support Appia, the Eurosystem’s initiative to develop a blueprint for Europe’s tokenized financial markets. The institutions warned that fragmentation could limit the benefits of tokenization and said the group may recommend ways for EU authorities to encourage firms to adopt its standards. In September, the Eurosystem launched Pontes, a system that allows financial institutions to settle wholesale transactions in tokenized assets in central bank money. Zcash devs propose another block time cut days after NU7 upgrade Zcash developers have proposed reducing the blockchain’s target block interval from 25 seconds to 20 seconds, seeking faster transaction confirmations days after activating the NU7 upgrade. On Sunday, developers ValarDragon and Evan Forbes submitted a draft Zcash Improvement Proposal (ZIP) on GitHub, saying that they want the change to be included in the next community poll and considered for the upcoming NU7.1 network upgrade. The reduction would shorten the expected wait for initial transaction confirmations. According to the proposal, this would improve the user experience for point-of-sale payments, exchange deposits and cross-chain swaps. The developers said the change would not increase the network’s overall daily capacity for private transactions. The proposal would also preserve Zcash’s existing issuance schedule, despite blocks being produced more frequently. The proposal comes just days after Zcash’s NU7 upgrade went live. On Friday, the NU7 upgrade was activated on the mainnet, cutting the network’s target block interval from 75 seconds to 25 seconds. The upgrade also introduced a Network Sustainability Mechanism designed to recycle a portion of transaction fees into future mining rewards while preserving Zcash’s 21 million ZEC supply cap.

articles.articleText: Çan2 Termik'in (CANTE) 3. çeyrekte zarar etti! Şirket zararının nedenlerini açıkladı - Çan2 Termik, 2026'nın ilk 9 ayında 3,79 milyar TL zarar açıkladı. Şirket; enflasyon muhasebesi, ertelenmiş vergi, PDVSA alacağının kırdırılması ve amortisman giderlerinin zararda etkili olduğunu bildirdi. Çan2 Termik A.Ş. (CANTE), 2026 yılı üçüncü çeyrek finansal sonuçlarını Kamuyu Aydınlatma Platformu'nda (KAP) açıkladı. Şirket, 1 Ocak-30 Eylül 2026 döneminde 3 milyar 792 milyon 199 bin 979 TL net zarar kaydetti. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Geçen yılın aynı döneminde 3 milyar 885 milyon 288 bin 42 TL zarar açıklayan şirketin dokuz aylık zararında sınırlı bir gerileme yaşandı. Üçüncü çeyrekteki net zarar ise 731 milyon 729 bin 19 TL oldu. CANTE zararının nedenlerini açıkladı Çan2 Termik, KAP'a yaptığı açıklamada dönem zararını etkileyen gider kalemlerine ilişkin bilgi verdi. Şirket, 30 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla 369 milyon 534 bin 100 TL FAVÖK ve 447 milyon 114 bin 995 TL net finansman geliri elde ettiğini bildirdi. Şirket, PDVSA alacağının kırdırılmasından kaynaklanan gider hariç olmak üzere, operasyonel olmayan ve nakdi/gayrinakdi risk içermeyen TFRS'ye uygun muhasebe kayıtlarının dönem zararını önemli ölçüde etkilediğini belirtti. Açıklanan gider kalemleri şöyle sıralandı: - Enflasyon muhasebesinden kaynaklanan zarar: 1 milyar 68 milyon 886 bin 155 TL - Ertelenmiş vergi gideri (VUK-TFRS farklılıkları): 910 milyon 252 bin 469 TL - PDVSA alacağının kırdırılmasından kaynaklanan gider: 1 milyar 726 milyon 663 bin 601 TL - Amortisman gideri: 1 milyar 95 milyon 959 bin 9 TL Bu kalemlerin toplamı 4 milyar 801 milyon 761 bin 234 TL'ye ulaştı. Şirket, söz konusu giderlerin finansal tablolardaki kâr/zarar kalemini önemli ölçüde etkilediğini ve 3 milyar 792 milyon 199 bin 979 TL ana ortaklık dönem zararının oluştuğunu açıkladı. PDVSA alacağı neden kırdırıldı? Şirketin açıklamasında, bağlı ortaklığı Denarius Pumping Services de Venezuela'nın Venezuela devlet petrol şirketi Petróleos de Venezuela S.A. (PDVSA) nezdindeki alacaklarına da değinildi. Söz konusu alacağın, Çan2 Termik'in Denarius'a iştirak etmesinden önceki döneme ait olduğu belirtildi. PDVSA'nın eski yükümlülüklerini yerine getirmemesi nedeniyle alacaklar için karşılık ayrılması yerine alacağın kırdırıldığı ve bu işlem sonucunda şirkete nakit girişi sağlandığı ifade edildi. Satışlar artarken faaliyet kârı negatife döndü Çan2 Termik'in satış gelirleri, 2026'nın ilk dokuz ayında geçen yılın aynı dönemine göre yüzde 4 artarak 6 milyar 139 milyon 116 bin 64 TL'ye yükseldi. Geçen yılın aynı döneminde satışlar 5 milyar 922 milyon 241 bin 278 TL seviyesindeydi. Esas faaliyet zararı ise 476 milyon 509 bin 690 TL'den 1 milyar 127 milyon 915 bin 912 TL'ye yükseldi. FAVÖK, geçen yılın ilk dokuz ayındaki 2 milyar 184 milyon 979 bin TL seviyesinden 536 milyon 939 bin TL'ye geriledi. Varlıklar ve özkaynaklar geriledi 30 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla şirketin toplam varlıkları 35 milyar 777 milyon 262 bin 515 TL oldu. 2025 yıl sonunda bu rakam 38 milyar 449 milyon 437 bin 121 TL seviyesindeydi. Toplam borçlar 2 milyar 687 milyon 664 bin 48 TL'den 2 milyar 801 milyon 958 bin 171 TL'ye yükselirken, özkaynaklar 34 milyar 727 milyon 65 bin 722 TL'den 32 milyar 729 milyon 178 bin 118 TL'ye geriledi. Şirketin piyasa değeri 10,29 milyar TL, PD/DD oranı ise 0,31 olarak kaydedildi.

articles.summaryTr: Astor Enerji, 2026'nın üçüncü çeyreğinde 3,17 milyar TL net zarar açıkladı. Şirketin 1,16 milyar TL'lik ortalama kâr beklentisine karşılık zarar etmesinde, 3,70 milyar TL'lik yatırım faaliyeti zararı etkili oldu.
articles.articleText: Astor Enerji'de (ASTOR) kar beklentisi tersine döndü: İşte şirketin 3. çeyrek bilançosu - Astor Enerji, 2026'nın üçüncü çeyreğinde 3,17 milyar TL net zarar açıkladı. Şirketin 1,16 milyar TL'lik ortalama kâr beklentisine karşılık zarar etmesinde, 3,70 milyar TL'lik yatırım faaliyeti zararı etkili oldu. Astor Enerji A.Ş. (ASTOR), 2026 yılı üçüncü çeyrek finansal sonuçlarını 9 Kasım 2026 tarihinde Kamuyu Aydınlatma Platformu'nda (KAP) açıkladı. Şirket, yılın üçüncü çeyreğinde 3 milyar 176 milyon 124 bin 858 TL net zarar kaydetti. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Matriks Haber tarafından düzenlenen bilanço anketine katılan 5 kurumun Astor Enerji için ortalama net kâr beklentisi 1 milyar 163 milyon 100 bin TL, medyan beklentisi ise 622 milyon TL seviyesindeydi. Şirket, kâr beklentilerinin aksine milyarlarca liralık zarar açıkladı. Yatırım faaliyetlerinden 3,7 milyar TL zarar Astor Enerji'nin üçüncü çeyrekte açıkladığı zararda yatırım faaliyetlerinden kaynaklanan 3 milyar 704 milyon 609 bin 274 TL'lik zarar etkili oldu. Şirket, 1 Ocak-30 Eylül 2026 döneminde toplam 1 milyar 677 milyon 318 bin 569 TL net kâr açıkladı. Geçen yılın aynı döneminde 6 milyar 174 milyon 499 bin 575 TL net kâr elde edilmişti. Böylece dokuz aylık net kâr yıllık bazda yüzde 73 geriledi. Satışlar ve faaliyet kârı arttı Şirketin satış gelirleri, 2026'nın ilk dokuz ayında geçen yılın aynı dönemine göre yüzde 16 artarak 33 milyar 622 milyon 133 bin 145 TL'ye yükseldi. 2025'in ilk dokuz ayında satışlar 28 milyar 875 milyon 710 bin 773 TL seviyesindeydi. Esas faaliyet kârı yüzde 31 artışla 10 milyar 941 milyon 317 bin 451 TL'ye çıkarken, FAVÖK 9 milyar 353 milyon 557 bin TL'den 11 milyar 569 milyon 635 bin TL'ye yükseldi. Borçlar yükseldi, özkaynaklar geriledi 30 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla Astor Enerji'nin toplam varlıkları 75 milyar 313 milyon 904 bin 731 TL oldu. 2025 yıl sonunda bu rakam 63 milyar 9 milyon 474 bin 750 TL seviyesindeydi. Toplam borçlar 21 milyar 636 milyon 539 bin 175 TL'den 34 milyar 438 milyon 845 bin 42 TL'ye yükseldi. Özkaynaklar ise 41 milyar 372 milyon 935 bin 575 TL'den 40 milyar 875 milyon 59 bin 689 TL'ye geriledi. Şirketin özkaynakları çeyreklik dönemde yüzde 12 azaldı. ASTOR hisse çarpanları Astor Enerji'nin piyasa değeri 154,79 milyar TL olarak açıklanırken, fiyat/kazanç (F/K) oranı 30,73, piyasa değeri/defter değeri (PD/DD) oranı ise 3,79 seviyesinde bulunuyor.

articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
articles.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
articles.titleTr: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
articles.summaryTr: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
articles.articleText: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026. Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect. In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife. The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models. "Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right. Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand. It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them. The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little. But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately. For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech. "President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year. It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way. - Could this be the end of 'Jensanity' - Published16 hours ago The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others. We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work. China denies that she was engaged in espionage. Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies. China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest. Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations. Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy. He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him. Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients. But can he survive? At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus. Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either. An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one. And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out. Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy. He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end. While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings. And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.
