items.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
items.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
items.summaryTr: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
items.articleText: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise. In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON. For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared. Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011. And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK. As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between. America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels. Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet. The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills? Two decisions On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil. Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security. Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas. Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations. Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable. At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama. But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt." "We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy." There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it. The case for drilling Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!" Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field. Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks. The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills". "If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice. Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress. But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets." Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had." Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead. Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption. And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another. With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination. The case for electrons The alternative is to build. Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel. The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables. The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs. Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power. And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills. All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills. The China question And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars. And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember. The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on. I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market". Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said. Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering. "There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was. Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs. Foreign investment, then - just not from China. Role reversal Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C. China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early. And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo. If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin. At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama. But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt." "We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy." There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it. The case for drilling Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!" Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field. Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks. The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills". "If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice. Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress. But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets." Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had." Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead. Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption. And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another. With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination. The case for electrons The alternative is to build. Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel. The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables. The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs. Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power. And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills. All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills. The China question And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars. And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember. The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on. I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market". Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said. Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering. "There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was. Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs. Foreign investment, then - just not from China. Role reversal Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C. China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early. And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo. If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin. items.titleTr: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
items.summaryTr: The US president said he spoke with Jensen Huang on Monday and asked him about the affair with the alleged spy.
items.articleText: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy - Published Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the boss of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy. The US President said he spoke with chief executive Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China". Nvidia, who has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off the value of Nvidia during trading on Monday as the firm's share price fell by about 4%. Trump later told reporters at the White House that the FBI was now looking into the issue, but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched. The FBI declined to comment when contacted the BBC. US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia, the company at the centre at the development of AI worldwide through its microchips. The American firm run, co-founded by Huang, is also a major focus in the AI rivalry between the US and China, with Washington officials treating the company's exports to Beijing as a matter of national security. 'He said he had no idea she was a spy' At the White House, Trump was asked multiple times, including by the BBC, on when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific. Trump said he thought Huang was an "honorable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations. "I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president said. He said he spoke with Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing, and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy". Trump added he was "sure" China president Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met. Huang has admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched. Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week. In the letter, the chairmen of the committees said they were seeking a briefing "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang". It is unclear whether Huang will appear. The BBC has contacted Nvidia and the committees. - What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published29 minutes ago - Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published2 hours ago Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent. It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today. Its chips have become so valuable to the AI-build out that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold. The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US. But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology. In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

items.summaryTr: The billionaire tech executive finds himself mired in a personal and national security scandal.
items.articleText: What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy - Published One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation. US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. On Sunday, Huang admitted, external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair. The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign. "I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters. Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. - Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy - Published22 minutes ago - Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published2 hours ago Who is Alice Huang and what do we know about the affair? US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported, external. Her current whereabouts are unknown. Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked. However, the BBC understands Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking". It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment. When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC. China has rejected the spying allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China." The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf. Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times. Why does it matter? Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race, which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers. Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China. Who is Jensen Huang? Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech", he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff. He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country". What is Nvidia and how important is it? Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games. Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates. Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch. "Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC. Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips. Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever. For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team". Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy. His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles. Who is Jensen Huang's wife? Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer. In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn. Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University. Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him". "He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney - Published21 September

He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy. His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles. Who is Jensen Huang's wife? Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer. In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn. Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University. Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him". "He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney - Published21 September

items.titleTr: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
items.summaryTr: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process next year.
items.articleText: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth - Published A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution. "By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorisation, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said. The effort will likely fail, as Republicans remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says the effort is aimed at pushing President Donald Trump to replace Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process. Hegseth has called the impeachment effort a "sham" and defended his record. "You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said in a video statement last week. "It's not going to work. We will not back down." He called Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" and said he was not concerned about the impeachment effort. In the video, Hegseth defended his leadership of the department and listed ways he has fulfilled Trump's America First agenda. Massie formally introduced his articles of impeachment in a resolution on the House floor on Monday afternoon. The move starts a 48-hour clock for the chamber to take up the measure. Lawmakers could vote on the resolution directly, vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside. "I'm doing this because it's the right thing to do," he told reporters after introducing the articles. Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, has been critical of Trump and the war in Iran since it started nearly nine months ago. He has previously garnered headlines over demanding the Trump administration release the files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and has now brought them back in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said the effort was aimed at preventing a Democrat spectacle next year when they have control of Congress. He said he hoped to force Trump to name a replacement, who could be quickly confirmed while Republicans have power. "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials." Democratic leadership has signalled openness to such an effort against Hegseth once they take control in January. Asked about the effort on Monday, Hegseth said, "We're not worried about that". He said he planned to hold a news conference on Tuesday to discuss the subject. Impeaching a cabinet secretary is rare. It must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. Trump was impeached by the House twice in his first term in office but was cleared by the Senate after two trials and not removed. As with the presidential process, the House would first hold a vote on charges against Hegseth and the Senate then would conduct a trial to decide whether to acquit or convict. The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not convict either one. While impeachment has been "an incredibly rare process", it has become far more normalised since the House impeached President Bill Clinton in 1998, said Paul Gowder, a law professor at Northwestern University in Chicago. He said it has become "much more common as the country has become more politically polarised," adding a prediction that several more of Trump's cabinet members may face impeachment over the next two years. Massie told reporters he was not sure if the measure had sufficient backing to pass. It would need a majority to pass the House and even with all Democratic support, it would still likely need some Republican support as the party holds a slim majority. Peter Loge, a professor of public affairs at George Washington University, told the BBC that he believed it was likely to pass due to those slim margins. "There are enough angry Republicans that more than enough Republicans are gonna simply not show up to vote," he said. Currently, there are 218 Republicans and 214 Democrats in the House. While the House requires a simple majority to pass articles of impeachment, the Senate mandates a two-thirds vote to convict, threshold that is difficult to meet in the current congressional term. When Democrats take over in January, they are likely to have at least 54 Senate seats - though two races do not yet have winners due to slim voting margins. A total of 60 votes will be required to convict and remove an official from office. Related topics - Published22 hours ago

items.summary: The ruling means the case can move forward, possibly with reduced charges in a new trial.

items.titleTr: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case
items.summaryTr: The ruling means the case can move forward, possibly with reduced charges in a new trial.
items.articleText: Judge denies motion to dismiss Lindsay Clancy's murder case - Published A Massachusetts judge has denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of killing her three children. The judge's ruling follows her defence team's request to dismiss the case after the 12-person jury in her September trial failed to reach a verdict. Clancy has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional. The ruling clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the case. They could reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether. Clancy's defence team argued to dismiss the case against her due to double jeopardy - a legal standard that prevents a person from being tried for the same crime twice. Her lawyers argued that Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the 26-day jury trial last summer, acted prematurely when he declared a mistrial on 4 September, saying that he should have sought a viable alternative. The five-week trial, its lead-up and aftermath gripped Americans, and put postpartum mental health issues such as psychosis in the spotlight. In his ruling on Monday, Sullivan said that a retrial would not unconstitutionally subject Clancy to double jeopardy, according to court documents obtained by the BBC. The possibility that "an unreasonably stubborn or eccentric juror" could be seated is "an unavoidable risk of the jury system", he said. "Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury's deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy's right not to be placed in double jeopardy." Sullivan also denied a defence motion to see records of the lone holdout juror in the case and to question the juror under oath. He said the defence failed to demonstrate that the records were needed for Clancy's defence at any retrial, and that questioning the juror "would have been impermissibly coercive". The judge has marked 16 November to discuss scheduling a potential second trial. He previously suggested it could begin in March. The BBC has contacted Clancy's lawyers for comment. Prosecutors in the closely watched case alleged that on 24 January 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all of her children - Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, eight months - in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home. After weeks of emotional testimony, the jury took a week to deliberate, repeatedly telling the judge that they could not reach a verdict. The deadlock stemmed from a lone juror who voted to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, while the 11 other jurors intended to acquit Clancy by reason of insanity. In Massachusetts, as well as in all US criminal murder trials, juries must reach a unanimous decision to convict or acquit a defendant. Because the jurors failed to unanimously agree on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law, the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September, which means that she was neither found guilty nor not guilty. Clancy is currently being housed in a state-run psychiatric hospital and medical facility in Massachusetts. Ana Faguy contributed reporting.

items.articleText: Dana White declines Trump’s offer to be White House press secretary Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White declined President Donald Trump's offer to be the next White House press secretary during a briefing on Monday. The president had asked White to take over the role in a social post over the weekend. Trump later said he was "having a little fun". During the briefing, White confirmed he won't take the job as he doesn't "want to be in politics."

items.articleText: Trump'tan İran açıklaması: "Şu aşamada askeri müdahale gerekli görünmüyor" YAYIN TARİHİ, 10 Kasım 2026 01:26 PAYLAŞ - ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, İran'a yönelik askeri müdahalenin şu an için gerekli görünmediğini söyledi. Trump, koşulların değişmesi halinde ABD ordusunun harekete geçmeye hazır olduğunu belirtti. ABD Başkanı Donald Trump, İran'la yaşanan çatışmaya ilişkin yaptığı açıklamada, şu aşamada ABD'nin askeri müdahalede bulunmasına gerek olmadığını düşündüğünü söyledi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle 9 Kasım Pazartesi günü gazetecilerin sorularını yanıtlayan Trump, "Bu noktada askeri harekât çok gerekli bir şey gibi görünmüyor. Ancak herhangi bir nedenle koşullar değişirse harekete geçmeye hazırız" ifadelerini kullandı. "Çatışmanın yakında sona ereceğini düşünüyorum" Trump, Tahran yönetimiyle yaşanan çatışmanın seyrine ilişkin de değerlendirmede bulundu. ABD Başkanı, "Bunun oldukça yakında sona ereceğini düşünüyorum" dedi. Trump'ın açıklamaları, Washington yönetiminin İran'a yönelik askeri seçenekleri tamamen dışlamadığını, ancak mevcut koşullarda doğrudan müdahaleyi gerekli görmediğini ortaya koydu.

items.articleText: ABD'den İsrail'e para musluğu kapanıyor! Rubio'dan dikkat çeken açıklama - ABD Dışişleri Bakanı Marco Rubio, İsrail'in finansal açıdan yeterli seviyeye ulaştığını belirterek Washington yönetiminin Tel Aviv'e artık finansman sağlamasına gerek kalmadığını söyledi. İki ülke arasında yeni bir savunma mutabakatı üzerinde görüşmeler sürüyor. ABD Dışişleri Bakanı Marco Rubio, Fransa'nın başkenti Paris'te düzenlenen G7 Dışişleri Bakanları toplantısının ardından yaptığı açıklamada, ABD'nin İsrail'e yönelik askeri finansman politikasında değişikliğe gidilebileceğinin sinyalini verdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Rubio, ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın beklentisinin İsrail'in artık kendi finansmanını karşılayabilecek ekonomik güce ulaştığı yönünde olduğunu belirtti. Rubio, "Başkanın beklentisi, İsrail'in artık yeterince refah düzeyine ve zenginliğe ulaştığı, dolayısıyla sadece 'satış' modeline geçebileceği yönünde. Bizden silah alabilir ama artık finansman sağlamamız gerekmiyor. Zaten bu, bizzat İsrail tarafının bize önerdiği bir husus" dedi. ABD ile İsrail arasında yeni savunma anlaşması görüşmeleri ABD ve İsrail'in yeni bir mutabakat zaptı üzerinde müzakereler yürüttüğünü aktaran Rubio, İsrail'in de kendi silahlarını ürettiğine dikkat çekti. Rubio, iki ülkenin bazı savunma kalemlerinde ortak üretim modeline geçebileceğini ifade etti. Rubio'dan Hegseth'e destek Rubio, ABD Savunma Bakanı Pete Hegseth'in görevden alınabileceğine ilişkin iddialar hakkında da konuştu. Hegseth'in İran'la savaşı destekleyen isimlerden biri olduğu yönündeki değerlendirmeler ve Trump'ın kendisini görevden almayı düşündüğü iddiaları hatırlatılan Rubio, savunma bakanına destek verdi. Rubio, Hegseth'in görevinde "çok iyi iş çıkardığını" düşündüğünü söyledi. Yapay zekanın ekonomik etkilerine dikkat çekti Rubio, yapay zekanın sağladığı fırsatların yanı sıra güvenlik ve ekonomi alanlarında ciddi riskler barındırdığını belirtti. Yapay zekanın biyolojik ve kimyasal silah üretiminde, siber saldırılarda ve terör eylemlerinde kullanılabileceğine ilişkin endişelerini dile getiren Rubio, teknolojinin iş gücü üzerindeki etkilerine de dikkat çekti. Rubio, yapay zekanın ekonomik faydalar sağlayacağını ancak bazı sektörleri ve çalışanları devre dışı bırakma potansiyeli bulunduğunu söyledi. Küresel kurumların yapay zekanın gelişimini yavaşlatacak düzenlemeler arayışında olduğunu savunan Rubio, bu yaklaşımdan endişe duyduğunu ve doğru bulmadığını ifade etti.

İki ülke arasında yeni bir savunma mutabakatı üzerinde görüşmeler sürüyor. ABD Dışişleri Bakanı Marco Rubio, Fransa'nın başkenti Paris'te düzenlenen G7 Dışişleri Bakanları toplantısının ardından yaptığı açıklamada, ABD'nin İsrail'e yönelik askeri finansman politikasında değişikliğe gidilebileceğinin sinyalini verdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Rubio, ABD Başkanı Donald Trump'ın beklentisinin İsrail'in artık kendi finansmanını karşılayabilecek ekonomik güce ulaştığı yönünde olduğunu belirtti. Rubio, "Başkanın beklentisi, İsrail'in artık yeterince refah düzeyine ve zenginliğe ulaştığı, dolayısıyla sadece 'satış' modeline geçebileceği yönünde. Bizden silah alabilir ama artık finansman sağlamamız gerekmiyor. Zaten bu, bizzat İsrail tarafının bize önerdiği bir husus" dedi. ABD ile İsrail arasında yeni savunma anlaşması görüşmeleri ABD ve İsrail'in yeni bir mutabakat zaptı üzerinde müzakereler yürüttüğünü aktaran Rubio, İsrail'in de kendi silahlarını ürettiğine dikkat çekti. Rubio, iki ülkenin bazı savunma kalemlerinde ortak üretim modeline geçebileceğini ifade etti. Rubio'dan Hegseth'e destek Rubio, ABD Savunma Bakanı Pete Hegseth'in görevden alınabileceğine ilişkin iddialar hakkında da konuştu. Hegseth'in İran'la savaşı destekleyen isimlerden biri olduğu yönündeki değerlendirmeler ve Trump'ın kendisini görevden almayı düşündüğü iddiaları hatırlatılan Rubio, savunma bakanına destek verdi. Rubio, Hegseth'in görevinde "çok iyi iş çıkardığını" düşündüğünü söyledi. Yapay zekanın ekonomik etkilerine dikkat çekti Rubio, yapay zekanın sağladığı fırsatların yanı sıra güvenlik ve ekonomi alanlarında ciddi riskler barındırdığını belirtti. Yapay zekanın biyolojik ve kimyasal silah üretiminde, siber saldırılarda ve terör eylemlerinde kullanılabileceğine ilişkin endişelerini dile getiren Rubio, teknolojinin iş gücü üzerindeki etkilerine de dikkat çekti. Rubio, yapay zekanın ekonomik faydalar sağlayacağını ancak bazı sektörleri ve çalışanları devre dışı bırakma potansiyeli bulunduğunu söyledi. Küresel kurumların yapay zekanın gelişimini yavaşlatacak düzenlemeler arayışında olduğunu savunan Rubio, bu yaklaşımdan endişe duyduğunu ve doğru bulmadığını ifade etti.

items.articleText: Here’s what happened in crypto today Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation. Today in crypto, Elliptic said North Korean hackers used memecoins to launder funds stolen in the Binance hack, EU authorities asked the finance industry to develop common standards for tokenized securities, and Zcash developers proposed cutting block times from 25 to 20 seconds. North Korean hackers create memecoins to launder funds from Binance hack: Elliptic North Korean hackers created memecoins to launder cryptocurrency stolen in the $6.3 billion Binance hack, routing roughly $430,000 through six newly launched tokens on the NEAR blockchain, according to a report from blockchain analytics firm Elliptic. Between Nov. 5 and 7, the hackers created at least six tokens on NEAR and used liquidity pools on decentralized exchanges to move stolen funds between wallets, Elliptic said. The tokens attracted almost no outside trading and were abandoned shortly after launch. The hackers used one set of wallets to swap stolen NEAR tokens for the new memecoins, then used another set to sell those memecoins back into the pools for NEAR. The swaps let them move funds without direct wallet-to-wallet transfers, though the transactions remained traceable onchain. Elliptic said the same laundering technique was also used following the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in 2025, when North Korean-linked actors moved at least $24 million through a newly created token on the TRON blockchain. EU taps industry to set standards for tokenized securities The European Central Bank, European Commission and European Securities and Markets Authority are seeking nominations for an industry-led group that will draft common standards for holding and settling tokenized securities. Eligible applicants include EU industry associations, global institutions, private firms and fintech companies. They can apply to the European Tokenisation Standards Group (ETSG) by Nov. 27, with work set to begin in January 2027, according to a release published Monday. The three EU institutions will participate as observers. The group will develop technical and market standards to help companies hold and settle tokenized securities across different distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms and ensure those platforms can work with existing financial systems. The group aims to produce an initial set of standards by early 2028, according to its mandate. The standards will support Appia, the Eurosystem’s initiative to develop a blueprint for Europe’s tokenized financial markets. The institutions warned that fragmentation could limit the benefits of tokenization and said the group may recommend ways for EU authorities to encourage firms to adopt its standards. In September, the Eurosystem launched Pontes, a system that allows financial institutions to settle wholesale transactions in tokenized assets in central bank money. Zcash devs propose another block time cut days after NU7 upgrade Zcash developers have proposed reducing the blockchain’s target block interval from 25 seconds to 20 seconds, seeking faster transaction confirmations days after activating the NU7 upgrade. On Sunday, developers ValarDragon and Evan Forbes submitted a draft Zcash Improvement Proposal (ZIP) on GitHub, saying that they want the change to be included in the next community poll and considered for the upcoming NU7.1 network upgrade. The reduction would shorten the expected wait for initial transaction confirmations. According to the proposal, this would improve the user experience for point-of-sale payments, exchange deposits and cross-chain swaps. The developers said the change would not increase the network’s overall daily capacity for private transactions. The proposal would also preserve Zcash’s existing issuance schedule, despite blocks being produced more frequently. The proposal comes just days after Zcash’s NU7 upgrade went live. On Friday, the NU7 upgrade was activated on the mainnet, cutting the network’s target block interval from 75 seconds to 25 seconds. The upgrade also introduced a Network Sustainability Mechanism designed to recycle a portion of transaction fees into future mining rewards while preserving Zcash’s 21 million ZEC supply cap.

items.articleText: Çan2 Termik'in (CANTE) 3. çeyrekte zarar etti! Şirket zararının nedenlerini açıkladı - Çan2 Termik, 2026'nın ilk 9 ayında 3,79 milyar TL zarar açıkladı. Şirket; enflasyon muhasebesi, ertelenmiş vergi, PDVSA alacağının kırdırılması ve amortisman giderlerinin zararda etkili olduğunu bildirdi. Çan2 Termik A.Ş. (CANTE), 2026 yılı üçüncü çeyrek finansal sonuçlarını Kamuyu Aydınlatma Platformu'nda (KAP) açıkladı. Şirket, 1 Ocak-30 Eylül 2026 döneminde 3 milyar 792 milyon 199 bin 979 TL net zarar kaydetti. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Geçen yılın aynı döneminde 3 milyar 885 milyon 288 bin 42 TL zarar açıklayan şirketin dokuz aylık zararında sınırlı bir gerileme yaşandı. Üçüncü çeyrekteki net zarar ise 731 milyon 729 bin 19 TL oldu. CANTE zararının nedenlerini açıkladı Çan2 Termik, KAP'a yaptığı açıklamada dönem zararını etkileyen gider kalemlerine ilişkin bilgi verdi. Şirket, 30 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla 369 milyon 534 bin 100 TL FAVÖK ve 447 milyon 114 bin 995 TL net finansman geliri elde ettiğini bildirdi. Şirket, PDVSA alacağının kırdırılmasından kaynaklanan gider hariç olmak üzere, operasyonel olmayan ve nakdi/gayrinakdi risk içermeyen TFRS'ye uygun muhasebe kayıtlarının dönem zararını önemli ölçüde etkilediğini belirtti. Açıklanan gider kalemleri şöyle sıralandı: - Enflasyon muhasebesinden kaynaklanan zarar: 1 milyar 68 milyon 886 bin 155 TL - Ertelenmiş vergi gideri (VUK-TFRS farklılıkları): 910 milyon 252 bin 469 TL - PDVSA alacağının kırdırılmasından kaynaklanan gider: 1 milyar 726 milyon 663 bin 601 TL - Amortisman gideri: 1 milyar 95 milyon 959 bin 9 TL Bu kalemlerin toplamı 4 milyar 801 milyon 761 bin 234 TL'ye ulaştı. Şirket, söz konusu giderlerin finansal tablolardaki kâr/zarar kalemini önemli ölçüde etkilediğini ve 3 milyar 792 milyon 199 bin 979 TL ana ortaklık dönem zararının oluştuğunu açıkladı. PDVSA alacağı neden kırdırıldı? Şirketin açıklamasında, bağlı ortaklığı Denarius Pumping Services de Venezuela'nın Venezuela devlet petrol şirketi Petróleos de Venezuela S.A. (PDVSA) nezdindeki alacaklarına da değinildi. Söz konusu alacağın, Çan2 Termik'in Denarius'a iştirak etmesinden önceki döneme ait olduğu belirtildi. PDVSA'nın eski yükümlülüklerini yerine getirmemesi nedeniyle alacaklar için karşılık ayrılması yerine alacağın kırdırıldığı ve bu işlem sonucunda şirkete nakit girişi sağlandığı ifade edildi. Satışlar artarken faaliyet kârı negatife döndü Çan2 Termik'in satış gelirleri, 2026'nın ilk dokuz ayında geçen yılın aynı dönemine göre yüzde 4 artarak 6 milyar 139 milyon 116 bin 64 TL'ye yükseldi. Geçen yılın aynı döneminde satışlar 5 milyar 922 milyon 241 bin 278 TL seviyesindeydi. Esas faaliyet zararı ise 476 milyon 509 bin 690 TL'den 1 milyar 127 milyon 915 bin 912 TL'ye yükseldi. FAVÖK, geçen yılın ilk dokuz ayındaki 2 milyar 184 milyon 979 bin TL seviyesinden 536 milyon 939 bin TL'ye geriledi. Varlıklar ve özkaynaklar geriledi 30 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla şirketin toplam varlıkları 35 milyar 777 milyon 262 bin 515 TL oldu. 2025 yıl sonunda bu rakam 38 milyar 449 milyon 437 bin 121 TL seviyesindeydi. Toplam borçlar 2 milyar 687 milyon 664 bin 48 TL'den 2 milyar 801 milyon 958 bin 171 TL'ye yükselirken, özkaynaklar 34 milyar 727 milyon 65 bin 722 TL'den 32 milyar 729 milyon 178 bin 118 TL'ye geriledi. Şirketin piyasa değeri 10,29 milyar TL, PD/DD oranı ise 0,31 olarak kaydedildi.

items.articleText: Astor Enerji'de (ASTOR) kar beklentisi tersine döndü: İşte şirketin 3. çeyrek bilançosu - Astor Enerji, 2026'nın üçüncü çeyreğinde 3,17 milyar TL net zarar açıkladı. Şirketin 1,16 milyar TL'lik ortalama kâr beklentisine karşılık zarar etmesinde, 3,70 milyar TL'lik yatırım faaliyeti zararı etkili oldu. Astor Enerji A.Ş. (ASTOR), 2026 yılı üçüncü çeyrek finansal sonuçlarını 9 Kasım 2026 tarihinde Kamuyu Aydınlatma Platformu'nda (KAP) açıkladı. Şirket, yılın üçüncü çeyreğinde 3 milyar 176 milyon 124 bin 858 TL net zarar kaydetti. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Matriks Haber tarafından düzenlenen bilanço anketine katılan 5 kurumun Astor Enerji için ortalama net kâr beklentisi 1 milyar 163 milyon 100 bin TL, medyan beklentisi ise 622 milyon TL seviyesindeydi. Şirket, kâr beklentilerinin aksine milyarlarca liralık zarar açıkladı. Yatırım faaliyetlerinden 3,7 milyar TL zarar Astor Enerji'nin üçüncü çeyrekte açıkladığı zararda yatırım faaliyetlerinden kaynaklanan 3 milyar 704 milyon 609 bin 274 TL'lik zarar etkili oldu. Şirket, 1 Ocak-30 Eylül 2026 döneminde toplam 1 milyar 677 milyon 318 bin 569 TL net kâr açıkladı. Geçen yılın aynı döneminde 6 milyar 174 milyon 499 bin 575 TL net kâr elde edilmişti. Böylece dokuz aylık net kâr yıllık bazda yüzde 73 geriledi. Satışlar ve faaliyet kârı arttı Şirketin satış gelirleri, 2026'nın ilk dokuz ayında geçen yılın aynı dönemine göre yüzde 16 artarak 33 milyar 622 milyon 133 bin 145 TL'ye yükseldi. 2025'in ilk dokuz ayında satışlar 28 milyar 875 milyon 710 bin 773 TL seviyesindeydi. Esas faaliyet kârı yüzde 31 artışla 10 milyar 941 milyon 317 bin 451 TL'ye çıkarken, FAVÖK 9 milyar 353 milyon 557 bin TL'den 11 milyar 569 milyon 635 bin TL'ye yükseldi. Borçlar yükseldi, özkaynaklar geriledi 30 Eylül 2026 itibarıyla Astor Enerji'nin toplam varlıkları 75 milyar 313 milyon 904 bin 731 TL oldu. 2025 yıl sonunda bu rakam 63 milyar 9 milyon 474 bin 750 TL seviyesindeydi. Toplam borçlar 21 milyar 636 milyon 539 bin 175 TL'den 34 milyar 438 milyon 845 bin 42 TL'ye yükseldi. Özkaynaklar ise 41 milyar 372 milyon 935 bin 575 TL'den 40 milyar 875 milyon 59 bin 689 TL'ye geriledi. Şirketin özkaynakları çeyreklik dönemde yüzde 12 azaldı. (ASTOR), 2026 yılı üçüncü çeyrek finansal sonuçlarını 9 Kasım 2026 tarihinde Kamuyu Aydınlatma Platformu'nda (KAP) açıkladı. items.titleTr: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
items.summaryTr: Jensen Huang is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
items.articleText: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond - Published The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026. Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect. In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife. The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models. "Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right. Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand. It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them. The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little. But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately. For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech. "President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year. It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way. - Could this be the end of 'Jensanity' - Published16 hours ago The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others. We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work. China denies that she was engaged in espionage. Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies. China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest. Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations. Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy. He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him. Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients. But can he survive? At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus. Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either. An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one. And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out. Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy. He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end. While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings. And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

items.title: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
items.summary: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.

items.titleTr: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028
items.summaryTr: Tyler Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the 2025 killing of the conservative activist.
items.articleText: Trial date of alleged Charlie Kirk killer set for June 2028 - Published The trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk, will start in June 2028, a judge has ordered. Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and six other charges in connection with the September 2025 killing of Kirk, 31, who was shot while he spoke at a Utah college campus. Utah County judge Tony Graf Jr on Monday told the court that jury selection would begin on 21 June, 2028. The prosecution has estimated the trial could last 17 weeks, while defence lawyers have said it could take seven months. Robinson could face the death penalty if found guilty of aggravated murder, something his defence team has sought to prevent. Prosecutors previously told the court they could be ready for trial by October 2027 but were willing to move that date back to January 2028 to avoid the holiday period. But defence attorneys said they needed more time to prepare their case and floated a 2029 start. As well as trying to stop Robinson facing the death penalty, they have also tried to have cameras banned from the courtroom. Kirk's widow, Erika, with whom he had two children, had pushed for as early a trial date as possible while also arguing proceedings should be live-streamed. She, along with Kirk's parents, Robert and Kathryn, have attended a number of court hearings in the case. At the end of Monday's proceedings, Erica Kirk's lawyer, Jeffrey A Nieman, told the judge that while "a trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie's assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family", they had "no choice but obviously to accept the schedule the court's put forward". Nieman added: "The family has waited long enough already; they should not have to wait any longer for this." During a five-day preliminary hearing in July, prosecutors outlined their evidence to show probable cause for trial. This included DNA allegedly tying Robinson to the murder weapon and other items recovered at the scene; confessions he allegedly made to loved ones; and a taped video statement from his roommate and romantic partner, Lance Twiggs. "There is a mountain of evidence that proves that he is the shooter," prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court in September. "We know that the defendant is the shooter… first, because of the video evidence; second, because of the DNA; third, because of his admissions; and fourth, because of circumstantial evidence," McBride said. Defence attorneys, meanwhile, have cast doubt upon evidence and expert witness credentials in the case.

items.summaryTr: Nvidia hisseleri, CEO Jensen Huang'ın yabancı istihbarat faaliyetinin hedefi olduğuna ilişkin iddialar sonrası başlatılan bağımsız soruşturmanın etkisiyle yüzde 7'yi aşan düşüşle açıldı. Hisseler daha sonra 175,9 dolara kadar geriledi.
items.articleText: CEO hakkındaki soruşturma yatırımcıyı kaçırdı: Nvidia hisselerinde yüzde 7'yi aşan düşüş! - Nvidia hisseleri, CEO Jensen Huang'ın yabancı istihbarat faaliyetinin hedefi olduğuna ilişkin iddialar sonrası başlatılan bağımsız soruşturmanın etkisiyle yüzde 7'yi aşan düşüşle açıldı. Hisseler daha sonra 175,9 dolara kadar geriledi. ABD'li çip üreticisi Nvidia'nın hisseleri, şirketin kurucusu ve CEO'su Jensen Huang hakkında gündeme gelen iddiaların ardından sert satış baskısıyla karşılaştı. Nvidia Yönetim Kurulu'nun bağımsız soruşturma başlatma kararı, yatırımcıların şirket yönetimine ilişkin endişelerini artırdı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Hisseler haftanın ilk işlem gününe yüzde 7'nin üzerinde kayıpla başladı. Türkiye saatiyle 19.30 itibarıyla Nvidia hisseleri yüzde 5'in üzerinde düşüşle 175,9 dolardan işlem gördü. Alice Huang hakkındaki iddialar soruşturmayı tetikledi ABD ile Çin arasında yapay zeka alanındaki küresel liderlik rekabeti sürerken, Jensen Huang'ın Çinli iş insanı Alice Huang ile yakın ilişkisi bulunduğu ve Alice Huang'ın Pekin yönetimine bilgi aktardığı yönündeki iddialar gündeme geldi. The New York Times'ta yayımlanan haberde, Jensen Huang'a yakın olduğu belirtilen Çinli iş kadını Alice Huang'ın Pekin yönetimine istihbarat amacıyla bilgi aktardığı öne sürüldü. Bu iddiaların ardından Nvidia Yönetim Kurulu, CEO Jensen Huang'ın yabancı istihbarat faaliyetinin hedefi olduğuna ilişkin haberleri incelemek üzere bağımsız soruşturma başlatacağını duyurdu. Huang soruşturmayla işbirliği yapacak Jensen Huang, çalışanlarına gönderdiği mesajda eşiyle ilişkisi konusunda sadık kalmadığını kabul ederken, yönetim kurulunun başlattığı bağımsız soruşturmayı desteklediğini açıkladı. Soruşturma sürecinde tam işbirliği yapacağını belirten Huang, "Nvidia'yı korumaya ve ABD'nin ulusal güvenliğini desteklemeye kararlıyım" ifadelerini kullandı. Soruşturmanın sonuçları ve Huang'ın CEO olarak görevine devam edip etmeyeceğine ilişkin belirsizlikler, yatırımcıların odağında bulunuyor.

items.title: Should you leave Australia to avoid paying 47% tax on crypto gains?
items.summary: Some Australian crypto investors are moving overseas to avoid the huge CGT increase from July 2027. But there are also less drastic ways you can pay less tax.

items.titleTr: Should you leave Australia to avoid paying 47% tax on crypto gains?
items.summaryTr: Some Australian crypto investors are moving overseas to avoid the huge CGT increase from July 2027. But there are also less drastic ways you can pay less tax.
items.articleText: Should you leave Australia to avoid paying 47% tax on crypto gains? Some Australian crypto investors are moving overseas to avoid the huge CGT increase from July 2027. But there are also less drastic ways you can pay less tax. In part one of our special on how to avoid Australia’s massive hike in capital gains taxes on crypto in July next year, we looked at borrowing against your Bitcoin or setting up a self-managed super fund (SMSF), among four ways to mitigate the impact of the taxes. While an SMSF offers Australians the greatest tax advantages, it’s only suitable for older investors, or those who are willing to lock up their crypto for decades until they retire. For younger investors, moving overseas could reduce your future crypto tax bills to 0% — but there are less drastic options to save on tax too. 5. Leave Australia and move to country with 0% CGT Australia’s impending tax changes have already inspired crypto king Fred Schebesta, founder of Finder.com, to become a tax exile in Singapore. From July, the top rate on real, long-term crypto gains will increase to 47%, minus the effects of inflation on the cost basis. For upwardly mobile, single crypto investors, the “nuclear option” of leaving the country to avoid giving almost half their gains to the government will look increasingly attractive. Many of the world’s top crypto hubs — Singapore, Portugal, Malta, UAE and Hong Kong — offer 0% capital gains taxes on long-term crypto gains in an attempt to attract wealthy investors. Also read: The one thing these 6 global crypto hubs all have in common...Should you leave Australia to avoid paying 47% tax on crypto gains? Ben Simpson, founder of crypto advisory service Collective Shift, says some of his members have already pulled the trigger. “Yeah, we’ve had a number of people that have sort of packed up and gone basically, ‘f—- this. I’m off to the Bahamas or whatnot,’” he says. Andrea Yuen, CEO of Sywftx, says she is keenly aware of the tax advantages of living outside of Australia. “I lived in Singapore for 30 years. I do miss my no capital gains tax,” she says. But she didn’t move there for tax reasons, and cautions that uprooting your life to avoid a bit of tax is a pretty drastic step. “I would never say that we should structure our lives only to think about tax outcomes,” she says. “There are many other wonderful reasons why I’ve come back to Australia and continued to live in Australia.” “I think if you’re moving countries solely based on a decision about whether you know your crypto is going to get taxed, then you probably need to think a little bit harder.” Simpson has considered the idea, given he already spends half the year in America looking after Collective Shift US, but looking into the rules put him off. “You really have to cut pretty much all ties to Australia. So if you are genuinely happy to leave and don’t want to come back for the majority of the year, and cut your healthcare and cut all your ties back to Australia, then that is a strategy.” “Bitcoin Jesus” Roger Ver gave up his US residency in 2014, and ten years later he was arrested and charged over failing to correctly report the value of his crypto holdings and paying exit taxes. He was forced to pay almost $50 million to make the case go away. Similarly, Australians leaving the country face a hefty exit tax on departure, which may require selling a decent amount of your stack. “They tax you on the way out. If you’ve got a lot of gains or profits you’re sitting on, they’ll catch you when you leave,” says Adrian Forza, director of Crypto Tax Australia. “Arguably it’d be bigger in the future, but it’s still difficult to stomach selling off everything to leave.” Forza explains you also have the option of paying the Australian taxes later on, but on the full value of the gain after you sell the asset. So if you expect Bitcoin to go up, you’d be best off paying the exit tax now. Related: Australia releases draft bill to adopt OECD crypto tax reporting framework 6. Set up a company to benefit from the company tax rate Simpson is only 27 and the prospect of locking up his crypto portfolio for forty years holds little appeal. Instead, he trades and holds crypto via a company to benefit from the 25% company tax rate. Running a single-person company is easier than you might think, but not worth the hassle unless you have a reasonable amount of capital and intend to make a lot of trades. It requires registering the company with ASIC and paying an annual fee, paying an accountant to produce financial statements and/or an annual company tax return and mucking about with payroll software and payday superannuation contributions if you plan to pay yourself an income. You can pay yourself a dividend at any time when you need some money. “The company structure is good if you’re wanting to cap the capital gains tax at the company tax rate,” he says, but notes there’s a big catch: when you take funds out of the company, you need to pay the difference between the 25% company tax rate and your personal tax rate. “You still need to pay your marginal income tax rates. If you’re on the top tax rate, like 47%,” he says. You may be wondering: if you have to pay your income tax rate anyway, which will equal the CGT rate from July, what is the benefit in paying a few thousand dollars and filling out a bunch of paperwork to run a company? Simpson explains that the key advantage is that while you are building up your crypto portfolio by trading in and out of different coins, you only pay the 25% company rate for each sale. That means paying up to 22% less than CGT each time you exit a position, which builds into an even more significant saving over time. “Instead of paying 47% because you’ve just taken the profits… then the CGT amount is only 25% — the company tax rate. So when you put that money back in, you’ve got more capital to play with.” However, if you don’t trade enough, it might be taxed at 30%. Forza says the advantages are greater for those on higher incomes. “If you’re a single person, then you’ve got a company, and you’re earning, you know, 150 grand a year, um, or over 200, then yeah, definitely a company would be the way to go, especially now that the CGT discount has gone out the window.” It’s not a particularly useful structure if you just plan to just hold your Bitcoin, however. There are some potential advantages but arguably not enough of them to be worth the hassle. 7. Just get out of crypto entirely to avoid high CGT rates The 50% CGT discount has been replaced by an indexation discount, which takes into account how much inflation affects how much you paid originally for an asset. This means that investors who buy and hold dividend stocks or index funds for a long period will receive a bigger CGT discount. So should you drop crypto and buy a bunch of ETFs so you can pay less tax? The short answer is no: the new CGT ‘discount’ is largely an illusion, as it simply measures your real gain after inflation. Simpson says crypto has been hit hard by the CGT changes, but it still offers the best risk-reward opportunity. “For us in Bitcoin, the growth ... heavily outweighs the tax considerations. In my point of view. If you’ve got the right portfolio, that can give you the right upside.” History suggests that despite volatility and years-long bear markets, the return from investing in Bitcoin over time would still leave investors ahead of ETF investors even after paying more tax. Investing further down the risk curve with altcoins however, can either pay off handsomely or end in total disaster. JPMorgan assumes that Bitcoin will compound by 10% on average in the years ahead. (Source JPMorgan/Bitcoin Archive) Simpson says he convinced his younger sister, who is a basketball player on a low income, to invest in Bitcoin two years ago rather than putting money into a savings account. “She’s up like 40% or 50% in her portfolio and she’s like, ‘wow, this is going to get me so much further towards buying a house one day than sitting in cash and losing 10% [to inflation over time],” he says. “That’s why I think Bitcoin makes so much sense to accumulate. And the tax considerations are not really there for most people I think.” Yuen says crypto is one of the few asset classes that offers investors the chance to make double-digit returns in a few months, or to potentially double their money. Even after paying the new taxes, crypto investors with those sorts of returns will still be ahead. “My dad always said to me, it’s a good thing, if you’ve made profits, you should be happy to pay some tax on it.” Well maybe not happy about it, but you’ll still be making money.
